entries.title: Amazon Says It's No Longer Using NDAs for Data Centers
entries.summary: The company announced it has stopped using secret agreements with county officials and acknowledges community backlash is leading to data center moratoriums across the country.
entries.content:
Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.

In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.

In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.

“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported on how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.

There has been a rush of recent local legislation attempting to address the secretive paperwork. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, and Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer have all cracked down on data center NDAs in recent executive orders. Multiple states, including New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Ohio, have considered recent legislation banning the practice.

At the federal level, a bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act in the House. Earlier this week, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), one of the bill’s sponsors sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle demanding information on their use of data center NDAs; Amazon told the Wall Street Journal that it was no longer using NDAs. (Google, Meta, and Oracle did not return the Journal’s request for comment.)

Amazon has been at the center of some high-profile controversies around NDAs. In Tucson, Arizona, Amazon was revealed last year to be the tenant of a controversial data center thanks to a public records request from a local outlet; an NDA had been in place barring county officials from sharing the identity of the end tenant. (Amazon has since exited that project.) In South Bend, Indiana, where the company has invested more than $13 billion into a massive data center campus, some elected officials have claimed that local government employees have been unable to answer questions about the project due to signing NDAs with the company.

Thanks to the opaque nature of data center financing and construction, end tenants like Amazon are often not the companies directly interfacing with government officials. As the Houston Chronicle reported last month, a top official in Wharton County, Texas, signed an NDA not with Amazon, but with contractor VisionFirst Advisors, which prevented him from sharing details about the Amazon project.

Amazon did not respond to WIRED’s queries about whether the promises around NDAs also extend to its contractors.

Much of the new blog from Garman is also dedicated to dispelling what he calls “misinformation and outright lies” around data centers and their water use, energy use, the use of diesel generators, and impacts on communities. “This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down,” he wrote.

As WIRED has reported, the idea that China is intentionally seeding widespread dissent and misinformation around data centers is a consistent message coming from the White House and tech leaders. Experts, however, say that this narrative is widely overblown, and that there is little evidence of Chinese misinformation driving the data center backlash.

entries.title: Best Smart Cat Trackers of 2026: Fi Mini vs. Tractive
entries.summary: After months of monitoring Basil’s activity and sleep, I found that Fi and Tractive cat trackers come with their own trade-offs.
entries.content:
A smart cat tracker is like a wearable health-monitoring device, such as a smart ring, smartwatch, or fitness tracker, that helps people stay on top of key wellness markers—but for a cat.

Why should humans have all the fun? In addition to live and historical GPS location tracking that helps any helicopter cat parent rest easy, the Fi Mini, Tractive Smart Cat Tracker, and Tractive Cat 6 Mini monitor your furry friend's health metrics, like activity and sleep. The collars also send alerts for changes in health patterns, such as when your pet is moving less or sleeping more than average, which can serve as early warning signs of potential health issues.

For the better part of the year, I've been testing these trackers on my cat Basil, analyzing each device's location accuracy, sleep- and activity-tracking capabilities, and health summary metrics. I also considered practical factors, such as ease of use, product size, and battery life.

If you have a cat that also goes outdoors, these trackers are much more reliable and comprehensive than something like an AirTag because they determine positioning via satellite instead of the nearest Bluetooth signal. They'll also notify you if your cat leaves your designated “safe zone.”

Ultimately, each smart tracker has its own strengths. The best model for you and your cat depends on your priorities—if you value long battery life, the Fi Mini ($99) is the best choice. If you want advanced health features, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini ($77) is the best smart collar option.

Be sure to check out our related pet guides, like the Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Automatic Feeders, and Best Pet Cameras.

In This Guide

Best Connected App

If tracking your cat's location is your top priority, Tractive (also called the Tractive Cat Mini) is the best option. Its historical heat maps show the areas your cat frequents, which is especially helpful for people with indoor–outdoor cats who roam large swaths of land.

However, note that all tested models rely on GPS for location tracking. This means that if the satellite signal is spotty—a common issue in rural areas and other settings—you may not know your cat's precise location. Some Reddit and Amazon reviewers complain that Tractive's location tracking is less accurate in areas with dense vegetation.

In setting up each tracker's connected app, you can designate specific mapped areas as safe or danger zones, and the app will notify you when the pet enters or exits these zones. Basil is an indoor cat, but with all three trackers, my apartment was too small to create a virtual fence around the perimeter, so I had to expand it to an area outside my apartment. That means if Basil got out but stayed nearby, I wouldn't get an alert.

In the Tractive app, after you create a profile, you'll get personalized daily activity goals for your cat based on statistics from other cats of similar age and weight. The app assigned Basil 120 to 230 minutes of daily activity and later reported that he was consistently more active than 70 percent of similar cats. I felt at peace knowing I'm keeping him on the move in my small apartment.

At the end of each day and week, the app provides activity averages and daily calorie estimates, calculated using factors like pet type, weight, and size, and compared with activity output.

Tractive's sleep-tracking feature monitors sleep duration, breaking it down into categories of night sleep, day sleep, and calm. Because it tracks sleep length and cycle phases based on movement patterns and time of day, the data is more general than precise. In general, I found the information in Tractive's app more useful and easier to analyze than in Fi.

Best Battery Life, Charging, and Size

Testing these trackers made me realize the importance of basic features like battery life and ease of removing the tracker from the collar for charging. This is where the Fi Mini shines. (Read my full review here.)

Fi Mini takes about two hours to reach a full charge, which lasted about two weeks in my testing. Fi claims four weeks, but two weeks is much longer than the Tractive, which conked out at around five days on a full charge. While I didn't test this, Fi claims its tracker can hold a six- to eight-week charge with the Fi Base add-on.

In addition to extending battery life by functioning as a connection source when your pet is at home, the Base also supposedly helps with location accuracy thanks to its Wi-Fi connection. One bonus for Fi users with an Apple Watch: You can add the Fi app to your watch to monitor your pet’s location and activity and enter “Lost Mode” without a phone, which is especially helpful if your cat has escaped while you're away from your phone.

The Fi's danger zone alerts were glitchy during my testing. On three occasions, I got notifications that Basil had left the safe zone (aka, my home and surrounding area). Each time, after I rushed home or raced to check my pet camera, I found him sleeping soundly on the living room couch. Other users have reported similar false alerts and location inaccuracy with the Fi.

Charging the Fi was a breeze. It uses the same USB-C charger as my iPhone, making the power-up process convenient and easy. The Tractive not only requires its own dedicated charger but also proved difficult to attach and detach from the device.

On the size front, the Fi Mini tracker is lightweight, small, and compact at just 1.5 x 1.0 x 0.5 inches. It comes with a strap loop and two types of soft cases. I liked the loop attachment best because its stretchy rubber material let me slip the tracker out without fully removing Basil's collar. Both the Tractive device itself and its collar attachment were much bulkier, and I worried they impeded Basil's ability to fully move his head downward.

The Fi Mini offers similar health metrics to the Tractive, but it only compares your pet's statistics against itself (as opposed to similar pets, like the Tractive). I liked that the Fi allows you to add vet records, receipts, and insurance information, and you can add vets to share pet-related documents and get appointment reminders.

Best Health Tracking Features

The Cat 6 Mini is the newest smart collar from Tractive (released earlier this year), now with advanced health features for respiratory and heart rate monitoring, as well as AI-powered weekly health summaries. I compared this new smart collar with the other smart collars I've tested, and although the short battery life is a pain, I recommend this model if measuring your cat's health metrics is your top priority. (Read my review here.)

Unlike the other models that use an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, the Tractive Cat 6 Mini device is the entire collar itself, and to charge, you need to remove the collar from the cat. As someone with reduced grip strength, the clasp made this task difficult for me. Like its predecessor, it also uses a proprietary charger. Charging took almost three hours, and it needed to be charged about every four days.

Like the previous model, you create a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Tractive also compares Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal. With the new Cat 6 Mini model, you'll get an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats, along with daily stats and weekly averages for sleep, activity, respiratory rate, and heart rate. Basil's respiratory rate was on the lower end, and his resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. The app even gave potential reasons and supplemental information for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures.” I'm planning to bring these stats and potential concerns to his next vet appointment.

Compare Our Picks

Also Tested

Moggie Activity Tracker + Hub for $149: The device not only provides metrics on your cat's health but also offers in-depth activity graphs with comparative baselines so you can see what's normal. I liked that it lasted a long time on a charge and was lightweight, small, and easy to take on and off without removing the entire collar. I live in a small apartment with limited outlets, so I also didn't love that the hub needed to be plugged in constantly for the device to work. But most of all, I don't think the device is accurately measuring activity metrics.

Is a Smart Tracker Worth It for Your Cat?

According to the American Veterinary Medical Association, about 10 million cats and dogs go missing each year in the US. While smart trackers aren't a silver bullet for preventing that problem, the data they provide can be helpful. Sure, you could technically use an Apple AirTag to track your cat—as I did for many years with Basil—but you'd have to hope it’s in range in an urgent situation. These smart health and GPS trackers are more accurate and alert you if your cat has escaped the “safe zone”—aka your home—especially helpful for indoor-only cats like mine. If your cat is indoor-outdoor, helpful heat maps trace regular routes, and you can add multiple safe zones so if your kitty ventures too far, you'll still be alerted. No matter which type of cat you have, these trackers allow you to follow your pet in real time when it matters most.

Plus, the health monitoring intel helps you better understand your pet's needs, routines, and normal patterns. Historical data comparisons can help identify warning signs of potential health issues, such as increased sleep or decreased activity.

There is a cost, though: A combination GPS tracker and smart health collar requires a subscription plan (see the individual reviews for more detail on rates), which is more expensive than a general tracker with no subscription required, like an AirTag. These smart trackers also require maintenance, such as frequent charging, firmware updates, and in-app monitoring. But I like to think of the devices as insurance—you hope you'll never need to rely on one, but in the event of an emergency, you'll be glad you invested. (Plus, it's fun to track your pet's metrics and understand a little more about their inner world.)

entries.title: Your Driverless Cab Is Spying on You
entries.summary: Self-driving cars from Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla are studded with cameras and sensors. Some of them are pointing at riders.
entries.content:
One afternoon this past summer, a self-driving Waymo pulled into a parking lot in San Mateo County, California, and stayed there until the police arrived. Local cops had gotten a 911 call from Waymo staffers—humans, it should be said—who were viewing the car’s passengers through cameras installed inside the vehicle. It looked like two teens were shooting a black handgun out the window of the vehicle, playing with it and drinking between shots, a police report said.

The story has a happy(ish) ending: The gun was shooting water-filled Orbeez, not bullets. But the incident drew attention to Waymo’s surveillance system. The cars are equipped with automated tech that can flag the presence of a firearm inside, the company said.

The outsides of self-driving cars are studded with cameras, which help them “see” the world around them. (Most also use other sensors, including radar and lidar.) Less appreciated are the cameras inside the vehicles, which companies say are essential to keeping riders safe and enforcing their rules. Earlier this year, Waymo said it used its cabin cameras to do both after some California passengers, many in their twenties or older, reported that Waymo employees suddenly took over the vehicles’ intercoms mid-ride to make sure they were old enough to ride on their own. (One 35-year-old told WIRED he thought his backpack sent up red flags.)

Still, robotaxi privacy policies can be broad. They suggest that footage captured inside vehicles can be used for many innocuous and commonsense reasons—to check cleanliness between rides, to detect lost items—but also to improve their products or services. These catch-all terms could cover many uses. Experts say that in the US, few clear rules govern this sort of surveillance, especially because riders often must agree to lengthy “terms of service” printed in minute fonts before they use ride-hailing apps. That leaves riders to trust that the companies are handling their information responsibly.

“We are being essentially abandoned by our lawmakers when it comes to consumer privacy and what companies can do with information after they’ve collected it,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where he works on surveillance and policing issues. His advice? “Just because you’re alone in the car doesn’t mean you’re alone in the car. You should behave as if there’s a jumpy person in the front seat.”

In general, robotaxi companies including Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla say that human staff view interior cameras only when needed. All say personal data, including recordings, may be sent to law enforcement or regulators. (A Waymo support page says that government agencies seeking data “are directed to follow valid legal processes in making such request.”)

But that doesn’t mean the interior cameras aren’t on and working. Waymo spokesperson Julia Ilina says the company uses “automated technology to support our teams in identifying potential violations.” A 2025 patent held by Waymo describes a system in which vehicles’ interior camera systems conduct automated "predetermined ride checklists” before, during, and after rides. (Ilina did not say whether that system is in use.)

Zoox’s website says its interior cameras “record the entirety of your ride.” This sort of personal data can be used to help operate rides, but also to develop and improve Zoox’s product. The company—owned by Amazon—says it might record conversations between riders and its support employees, but that it doesn’t save recordings. Zoox spokesperson

Whitney Jencks said the company had nothing more specific to share about its privacy policies.

Online documents for Tesla’s Robotaxi service say a green indicator shows up on the vehicle’s central touchscreen when the camera is activated. Riders can opt in to sharing in-cabin video and audio with the company through a toggle menu in the “data and privacy” section of its app. The documents also say riders in the company’s “early access” program automatically opt in to data sharing. The company didn’t respond to questions for this story, including whether that early access program has technically concluded. The company opened its Robotaxi app to the public in a handful of Texas and Florida cities in early September.

Cameras inside robotaxis make plenty of sense. “You need some kind of check on what people do in a car with no driver,” says Justin Brookman, who directs technology policy at Consumer Reports. “People are going to have sex in Waymos if there are no cameras.” (Media reports suggest that the cameras don’t always stop them.)

But the law hasn’t yet fully contemplated what companies should be able to see, save, and use. “These vehicles are relatively new, so there are no expectations around what’s appropriate,” Brookman says. “There should be some check in place.”

Auto companies don’t have the best record on data privacy.

In 2023, Reuters reported that groups of Tesla employees had, over several years, shared sensitive videos and images captured by owners’ cars. Shared recordings reportedly included a video of a man approaching a car while naked, and a violent collision between a car and a child on a bike. Tesla boasts that its years-deep repository of data from personal vehicles gives it an edge in developing autonomous vehicle software, and its privacy policy says camera recordings are kept anonymous. But former employees told Reuters that the system easily revealed where the images were recorded, which could have allowed them to link recordings to specific owners’ garages or driveways.

Earlier this year, General Motors paid California motorists nearly $13 million in penalties after the company was found to have sold driving data to brokers and eventually insurers without their consent.

“My big concern is that automakers love to collect data,” Guariglia says. “With autonomous vehicles, there’s even more data to collect. And the more data they collect, the more they’re going to find reasons to sell it.”

In the meantime, his privacy-related advice? Behave.

entries.title: Election Deniers Think the GOP’s Terrible Midterm Polling Is a ‘Psyop’
entries.summary: Dozens and dozens of high profile MAGA influencers and pundits have weighed in. “The laughable fake polls are rolling out,” Catturd posted on X.
entries.content:
Taking their lead from president Donald Trump, election deniers have dismissed the GOP’s terrible polling numbers by claiming the polls themselves are fake, a psyop, or a ploy to stop Republicans from turning out to vote in November.

Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, told Fox News that midterm election polling is a “psyop…to depress conservative turnout.”

“The midterms are near,” Phillip Buchanan, the election denier and MAGA troll known online as Catturd, wrote to his four million followers on X. “The laughable fake polls are rolling out.”

For over a decade, Trump has claimed without evidence that American elections have been impacted by fraud. In the wake of his loss in 2020, an entire online community and ecosystem of election denial groups sprung up to push the baseless allegation that former president Joe Biden stole the election from Trump. These claims have become central to the Republican Party’s belief system, to the point where hundreds of GOP candidates for federal and statewide elections in November have expressed doubts about the integrity of US elections.

And now, multiple polls have shown Trump’s approval rating at historic lows with Democrats leading in Senate races across the country in states Trump won easily in 2024. Reuters reported this week that Republicans are now pouring money into dozens of races they considered safe.

Trump has called polls fake 39 times since returning to the White House last year, according to analysis from media watchdog Media Matters for America, including nine times in August alone. In one post on Truth Social last month, he claimed the polls were “demoralization operations” designed by Democrats to stop Republicans from voting. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump again dismissed negative polling out of Iowa and stated: “The polls are fake.”

The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment, but as WIRED reported this week, Trump’s own aides are extremely concerned about the polling and the potential loss of both the House and Senate. “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed,” one longtime Trumpworld operative told WIRED.

While the White House may be worried, figures in the election denial community have repeated Trump’s claims about fake polls.

Steve Bannon, who has been among the loudest voices promoting election denial conspiracies for the last six years, also called the recent polling a “psyop,” adding: “I want to make sure everybody understands that our fate is still in our hands, no matter what the media is telling you, no matter what they're saying about a blue tsunami, a blue wave.”

Seth Keshel, a former Army colonel-turned election denial superstar who claims to have close ties to the White House, also branded the negative polls a “psyop,” adding on X: “Polling is so unethical now it should be outlawed.”

Some MAGA figures have conceded that the low polling numbers reflect the reality of Trump’s failure to keep his promises. When right-wing podcaster and election denier Tim Pool suggested Trump’s low approval rating was the result of high gas prices and the ongoing war in Iran, however, Bill Mitchell, a MAGA political commentator with over half a million followers on X responded: “Maybe it's fake polls.”

Dozens and dozens of high profile MAGA influencers have weighed in. “Polls are fake. All 50 States are Red,” Julie Donuts, a prominent booster of election denial conspiracy theories with 220,000 followers on X, wrote. The post was accompanied by an image of a map showing widespread support for Trump that comes from 2016.

Kambree Nelson, a MAGA influencer who worked for the America First Policy Institute and once suggested the moon had disappeared for a week, blamed the media for the fake polls, writing: “Theyre [sic] actually running the biggest scam of the election. Fake polls, puffball interviews, all designed to crush our spirit and keep us home. They’re terrified of the momentum they can feel building. Don’t fall for it.”

The Maryland Election Integrity Group, which promotes baseless election denial conspiracy theories, shared a post on X that claimed without evidence that “polling has been skewed to favor Democrats by three points on average over the last FIVE cycles.”

In recent weeks, some election deniers have even suggested that polls never actually take place. “52 years old. I have never been ‘polled’. Polls are fake to sway votes,” David Freeman, an election denier and pro-Trump influencer known online as Gunther Eagleman, wrote on X.

But as one of the top commenters on the post points out, Freeman has repeatedly shared polling that is favorable towards Trump, writing: “Gunther LOVES polls when they are in his favor.”

entries.title: A Flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac App Could Have Let Hackers Grab Sensitive Data
entries.summary: While the focus has been on AI agents’ hacking capabilities, a recently patched vulnerability in a ChatGPT app shows that AI software is itself an inviting—and vulnerable—target.
entries.content:
Hardly a day goes by lately without news of AI agents autonomously hacking websites or AI tools being used by cybercriminals and scammers. But a recently patched vulnerability in the macOS version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT underscores the potential value to attackers of compromising AI software itself as these apps proliferate more and more.

The bug could have been exploited to essentially take over ChatGPT on a victim’s computer, giving an attacker access to all the chat logs and other data stored by the app, as well as interconnections like browser sessions. Discovered by researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, the vulnerability illustrates the deep system access and trust that AI platforms are afforded in order to work—and the target that this puts on their backs.

“Agents need a lot of access to do their job,” says Objective-See Foundation software analyst and longtime macOS researcher Patrick Wardle. “They are like the building manager who has access to the keys to all the rooms. So if they can be corrupted or subverted, that’s super problematic. It can mean that unprivileged code could then potentially have access to all the things.”

OpenAI publicly acknowledged the security flaw and fix in its system change log on September 25. “We continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” OpenAI spokesperson Shane Bauer told WIRED in a statement.

The ChatGPT macOS app includes multiple components that communicate with each other securely by checking for digital signatures. The idea is to confirm with these validity checks that both processes are OpenAI components and not outside, potentially malicious software making a request. And the system design goes so far as to require these signature checks at three layers of remove from the request, to ensure that malicious software isn’t somehow directing an OpenAI component to be a proxy and make a seemingly trusted request.

Objective-See Foundation researchers found, though, that there is a trusted component, a script interpreter, that would accept an untrusted script (or list of commands to run) and could then be manipulated to deliver this script into the main ChatGPT process. “They also check the parent and grandparent of that process, but the malicious script just spawns the script interpreter three times and then makes the request so it will satisfy the requirements,” Wardle says.

The vulnerability was “insanely trivial” to exploit, he adds, and his proof of concept only required about a dozen lines of code. In addition to accessing ChatGPT chat logs, the vulnerability could also be used to get ChatGPT to run commands for the attacker, such as accessing a browser or other sensitive applications, with the requests appearing as legitimate instructions issued by the OpenAI software.

Wardle will present analysis of a number of AI macOS application bugs at Objective by the Sea, an Apple-focused security conference in November.

He recently found a flaw, now patched, in the dictation feature of Meta’s new Muse AI assistant that could have been exploited by a local attacker to grab a mishandled authentication token and gain access to user data. And he says that he has already submitted a new vulnerability finding to OpenAI related to the integration between ChatGPT and the company’s new always-on Dots AI assistant. OpenAI is currently reviewing his report.

“AI companies are fixated on adding features right now,” Wardle says. “But as always, the more features, the broader the attack surface. So all of these companies need to be fully focused on security, and from what I can see, it still often seems like an afterthought.”

entries.title: Health Care Workers Are Tired of Cleaning Up Palantir’s Mess
entries.summary: A hospital giant and radiology network turned to Palantir to streamline scheduling, but nurses and other staff say the new software is causing errors, burnout, and frustration.
entries.content:
Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.

Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.

“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.

The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.

As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.

Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.

HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”

Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”

Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds.

HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback.

“Being Kicked”

On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.

But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says.

Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology.

Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.)

Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry, a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations. Named after the beat-keeping musical instrument, it uses algorithmic forecasts of patient volumes and staffing needs to automatically build nursing schedules. When Timpani launched in 2023, HCA’s top innovation executive Michael Schlosser told WIRED it would save time and money, as well as eliminate favoritism in assigning shifts.

Schlosser said in a paper this past July that Timpani has drastically reduced the number of hours managers spend on scheduling each month, lowered reliance on costly contract nurses to fill shifts, and increased retention. “The efficiency comes from AI generating stronger initial schedules,” he wrote, adding that over 98 percent “include a mix of skill and experiences.”

HCA’s responsible AI policy emphasizes protecting individuals from “physical” or “emotional” harms, and executives have said they spoke to nurses and took an empathetic approach in developing Timpani. In marketing materials, the company features nurses praising the tool for being easy to use and saving them time. Yet other HCA nurses say they feel ignored and disrespected, and they are not the only health care workers who have raised concerns about Palantir’s push into their industry.

Rayus Radiology, a large US imaging chain, began receiving complaints about scheduling errors earlier this year after it introduced a tool also built on Palantir Foundry, according to internal documents viewed by WIRED. The software is designed to populate scheduling fields from doctors’ orders. But in a number of cases, it linked the requests to the wrong patient profiles, listed tests or scans that didn’t match the orders, or made up personal details about patients. Schedulers who work at Rayus suspect that non-standard forms, illegible handwriting, and insufficient human review contributed to the issues.

Rayus spokesperson Kit Crancer says “the broad characterizations” do not fairly reflect its “processes, safeguards, or commitment to safe, accurate, and timely patient care.” He adds that Rayus uses technology “to support, not replace, appropriate human judgment and oversight.”

A Palantir spokesperson declined to comment using their name, but the company has described its software as merely presenting information in a more helpful manner and emphasized that customers are responsible for the data, policies, and decisionmaking.

Palantir Anxiety

Palantir’s sales have nearly doubled recently to almost $2 billion per quarter, as organizations seek its help analyzing data and automating tasks. Soaring costs and staffing shortages have made health care providers especially eager customers. Cleveland Clinic credited Palantir software with boosting patient capacity by forecasting ER discharges and replacing manual coordination.

But Palantir has also received pushback from civil rights activists over its defense and immigration work, as well as the stated political views of cofounders Peter Thiel and Alex Karp. In the UK, Palantir landed a $440 million contract with the National Health Service to try to cut appointment wait times, but nurses and activists have demanded it be canceled over privacy and security concerns.

At HCA, some nurses also want Palantir gone. While studies show AI-based scheduling holds promise, nurses say Timpani has become a source of anxiety. “Everyone checks immediately and every month you hear, ‘Man, why did it schedule me like that?’” Barker says.

Initially, some local managers could edit Timpani’s schedules. Now, nurses must flag problematic shifts to a centralized team at HCA headquarters in Nashville, which reviews appeals without direct communication or room for explanation, according to nurses. If denied, they try to swap shifts, but the chances of success are about only 50 percent, Barker and Retzloff claim.

Barker, who is a National Nurses United leader at an HCA psychiatric center, claims several colleagues quit over Timpani and that workplace injuries have climbed in the first 12 months with the tool. The center’s union of about 500 nurses filed a grievance over the software, arguing HCA is failing to sufficiently honor scheduling preferences. The matter is likely headed to arbitration.

In Timpani’s early days, HCA’s Schlosser acknowledged health care workers can be slow to adopt tech “because they have people’s lives in their hands.” But he envisioned a future where frontline nurses actively pushed for more tools: “Then it’ll be fun.” Three years later, some nurses see little reason to rejoice.

entries.title: 31 Best STEM Toys for Kids (2026): Learning Made Fun
entries.summary: We found lots of math-filled and science-rich toys for tiny nerds to assemble, bake, squish—or even tear apart and rebuild.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Anyone who has ever watched a toddler methodically take apart a Tupperware drawer knows that many children are natural-born engineers. Your job as a parent is to nurture their creativity … and clean up the mess afterward. I've tested tons of STEM toys with my kids over the years, some with help from other parents on the WIRED Reviews team and some with help from my wife, who is a teacher and can road-test them in the classroom.

Wrap up a few of these STEM toys (also called STEAM toys; we love you too, arts!) for your future scientist to assemble, squish, or dismantle. Hopefully, they'll thank you for the early encouragement when they're older. Be sure to check out our assortment of other buying guides, including the Best Subscription Boxes for Kids, Best Speakers for Kids, and How to Build the Lego Collection of Your Dreams.

Updated September 2026: I've added Gravity Maze, an Engine-Building Kit, and Rush Hour Deluxe.

  • Creative Kit

    Plus Plus

    Mini Interlocking Building Blocks Set

    There’s something super-satisfying about these tactile building blocks. They come in a range of appealing colors and have a slightly squishy form that makes them delightful to build with and pull apart. Because the pieces are all the same, children don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block as they do with Lego. They can pick by color or just experiment, and it’s as easy to create bracelets and headbands as it is to construct robots and bridges.

    These building blocks were very popular in the classroom with 7- and 8-year-olds. Some kids had fun just playing without something specific in mind, while others planned scenes and put their engineering skills to use to realize them. There are also some instruction booklets with suggestions.

    For kids aged 5 years and up.

  • Sound Stage

    Qubs

    Qubitunes

    We’re in love with this screen-free play stage and

    speaker for kids. The cute wooden design includes a slot to insert a cartridge and a circular sound stage divided into four sections where you can pop characters on top to change the audio it plays. This basic functionality allows for a clever variety of add-on packs, from stories about quirky characters in the Groblies ($20) to a cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients. My favorite is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. The stereo speakers are quite good, it has a headphone port, and the Qubitunes can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. My wife has this in the reward area of her classroom, and it’s the most popular option with 7- and 8-year-olds.

    For kids aged 3 years and up.

  • Wind-Up Flashlight

    Ambessa

    DIY Kinetic Flashlight

    Kids can build this wind-up flashlight themselves and learn all about electronic components and kinetic energy in the process. The thoughtful design includes 10 separate parts, and there are 16 steps to follow to assemble it. No batteries are required, and the kit is designed to be easy to disassemble and use again, making it perfect for a classroom setting. Our testers were delighted that simply winding the completed flashlight brought it to life (three minutes of winding provides 30 minutes of light). For every kit purchased, the maker, Ambessa, donates one to a refugee child out of school.

    For kids aged 8 years and up.

  • Knight School

    Particula

    GoChess Mini

    I have been struggling for a few years to get my now 7- and 9-year-old interested in chess, and the GoChess Mini works wonderfully. This lightweight, portable board is beautiful to use—the pieces have a nice matte finish and are pleasingly weighty. Once you charge the Bluetooth-enabled board and connect it to the app, you can either play against remote players, against yourself, or get AI-enabled assistance to help guide your moves. You can scale the amount of assistance, whether it’s a little or a lot, and different-colored lights show you the advisability of different moves as you pick up each piece. One evening of charging results in weeks of playtime; my kids will play for hours and discuss each move as they go. It’s great.—Adrienne So

    Particula also offers a

    Harry Potter-themed GoChess Mini Board ($350) which appears in my best smart chess boards guide.

    For kids aged 6 years and up.

  • Marble-Powered Computer

    Upper Story

    Turing Tumble

    Turing Tumble is a wonderful way to teach kids coding fundamentals. It combines the simple pleasure of marble runs with a beautifully illustrated sci-fi comic book packed with challenging puzzles. The board resembles a pachinko game, and you have to slot in different pieces to divert the blue and red balls and get the required pattern at the bottom. My 9-year-old spent hours working through the puzzles, reconfiguring this marble-powered computer. As the challenges grew tougher, the whole family joined in to find solutions. Well-designed, satisfying, and rewarding, this is a good pick for most kids.

    For kids aged 8 years and up.

  • Coding Ball

    Sphero

    Bolt

    The Sphero Edu app is packed with computer science lessons and activities for different age groups. Bolt has an 8 x 8 LED board on top, various sensors inside (compass, light sensor, gyroscope, accelerometer), and supports infrared communication. My wife is a teacher and uses this in the classroom to teach basic coding skills, giving students challenges like navigating a maze. She says many kids grasp the concepts much faster than they might with a book or screen, because they can see the Bolt moving in physical space.

    For kids aged 9 years and up.

  • Marble Puzzle

    ThinkFun

    Gravity Maze

    Kids love marble runs, and ThinkFun combines the joy of dropping marbles with a clever logic puzzle design in Gravity Maze. There are 60 challenge cards ranging in difficulty, and you must figure out how to place the available pieces to build a 3D maze that guides the marble to your target tower.

    For kids aged 8 years and up.

  • Endless Building Fun

    Valtech

    Magna-Tiles

    The return on investment with Magna-Tiles staggers me. It's been years, and at 6 and 8 years old, my children can still occupy themselves with these for hours. Translucent Magna-Tiles click together to form both two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects. Younger kids can make a house with a backyard and fences, or ice cream cones. With an older kid, the sky is the limit—or, rather, your credit card is, since there are wheelbarrows full of expansion sets you can buy. My daughter can currently build a full village in an afternoon for her stuffed animals.

    If these are too pricey, there are alternatives that work just as well, like Picasso Tiles, which are

    $23 for 60 pieces. —Adrienne So

    For kids aged 3 years and up.

  • Robo Fun

    Robotical

    Marty the Robot V2

    Combining coding with robotics can be a great way of engaging kids, and Marty the Robot V2 is an irresistibly charming biped with nine servo motors inside that enable him to walk, kick, wave, sidestep, and even waggle his eyebrows. There’s a customized microcontroller inside, various sensors, Bluetooth connectivity, and a speaker, so there’s plenty of potential for kids to code various routines and an

    extensive knowledge base with lessons and tutorials. Robotical has designed Marty for kids of all ages, so at the basic level, you can use color cards (green to move forward, for example) to control him. Older kids can use Scratch, a simplified coding program with drag-and-drop blocks on a connected Android or iOS device, and when they’re ready to advance, they can move on to Python. Marty is cute and fun but very expensive, though it’s mainly geared toward use in schools, and there are lots of good resources for educators.

    For kids aged 5 years and up.

  • Construction Capers

    Geomag

    Classic Magnetic Building Set

    My entire household found this magnetic construction set irresistible, and there has been a new 3D structure on the coffee table every morning. The kit comprises glow-in-the-dark magnetic rods (crafted from recycled plastic), steel spheres, and plastic bases in different shapes. You also get storage boxes to put everything away in. There’s a guide in the box with a few suggested structures, but creating your own is a big part of the appeal. There are sets of various sizes.

    For kids aged 3 years and up.

  • Early Engineering

    National Geographic

    4-Cylinder Engine Building Kit

    You can build a four-cylinder engine with this 175-piece kit. It’s fun to assemble, but there are lots of fiddly pieces (tiny screws and springs), so younger kids may need supervision. Once built, simply insert three AA batteries (not included), push the button, and it comes to life, with moving pistons, valves, gears, and light-up LEDs to help kids understand how engines work. The instruction booklet also includes a brief potted history.

    For kids aged 10 years and up.

  • A Twist on a Classic

    Particula

    GoCube

    No one needs a Bluetooth-enabled Rubik's Cube, but once you get your hands on a GoCube you probably won't be able to put it down. Smart sensors inside the beautiful, glowing cube connect to a companion app on your phone and sense where each block is positioned. You can learn algorithms and strategies that will help you get your solve-time down. And if you give everyone you know a GoCube, you can also stage live competitions with friends and family! —Adrienne So

    For kids aged 8 years and up.

  • Sand Castles

    Kinetic Sand

    My kids love this moldable sand and have happily spent countless hours over the years making tabletop structures. It behaves like wet sand and never dries out, so you can shape it with your hands or use tools and molds to make castles. It comes in many colors and clumps together easily but doesn’t stick to your hands or surfaces. While it’s generally easy to clean up, it’s a good idea to confine play to a tray or table and supervise your kids, or you may end up picking tiny bits of pink sand out of your carpet.

    For kids aged 3 years and up.

  • Remote-Controlled Robot

    Wonder Workshop

    Dash

    This super-cute robot looks like it rolled straight out of a Pixar movie. With a big, expressive eye atop three balls, it zips around with real personality, which helps it successfully combine play and learning in a way that all educational STEM toys aim for but many fall short of. Dash has lived with us for several years now and of all the coding robots I've tried, it remains my favorite. It’s a durable toy that works on a simple level like a remote-controlled car, but it also ties in with various apps to play games, solve puzzles, and create programs. Lego connectors for Dash’s head add to the creative possibilities. Wonder Workshop also offers some optional accessories.

    For kids aged 6 years and up.

entries.content:
When I decided to take a last-minute ski trip, despite never having skied before, I went straight to Columbia. Was I shredding the slopes? Absolutely not, but at least I was warm, thanks to my Snowy Summit Insulated Jacket and Bugaboo II Pants. Here at WIRED, we’re fans of Columbia. The brand makes reliable, well-priced outdoor gear for skiing, hiking, hunting, or just a day at the beach. Plus, there’s almost always a deal to be found.

WIRED reviewer Chris Haslam loves the Columbia Konos Trillium ATR as a value-packed all-around trail-running shoe for faster hikes, day trips, and mixed-terrain excursions. The plush cushioning and 8-millimeter drop are ideal on packed dirt, gravel, and woodland paths. For hiking boots, he recommends the Tellurix Titanium OutDry, which are waterproof, provide serious traction on wet rock and mud, and are surprisingly lightweight at 1.6 pounds per pair.

With summer approaching, now’s the time to prepare for outings. If you’re eyeing snow gear, the off-season is when prices hit their lowest. I’ve gathered the latest Columbia promo codes to sweeten the deal.

Columbia Promo Code: 15% Off All Orders

Join Columbia’s Greater Rewards program—it’s free to sign up, and you won’t need a Columbia promo code—to get 15% off your first online order. Note that this coupon can’t be combined with any other Columbia discount code or deal and expires if not redeemed within 30 days of the date of issuance. Plus, as a member, you’ll earn points on purchases, get free standard shipping, and receive a 20 percent discount on your birthday.

Unlock Columbia Discount Codes and Get $20 off

Once you sign up for Columbia’s Greater Rewards program and opt in to email notifications, you’ll receive a unique Columbia coupon code for $10 off your online purchase when you spend $100 or more. If you subscribe to both email and text notifications, the single-use Columbia coupon will increase to $20 off your purchase of $100 or more.

Top Columbia Deals for Current Students

Active and retired military members, as well as first responders, are also eligible for a 10% discount. You must log in directly to ID.me and verify your status to receive the Columbia promo code.

Get Free Shipping With Columbia Codes

As a Greater Rewards member, you receive free standard shipping on all online orders with no minimum purchase required. As long as you’re signed in to your account, the Columbia free shipping code will automatically be applied at checkout.

Give More With the Columbia Gift Card

Not sure what to get the adventurer in your life? If your loved one is a nature enthusiast, you need a great grad gift idea for someone taking a gap year, or if the giftee is finally taking that backpacking trip, a Columbia gift card can be a thoughtful gift for many occasions. How to Apply Your Columbia Coupon Code

entries.title: Uber Eats Promo Codes: $15 Off│October 2026
entries.summary: Hunger meets savings. Discover verified Uber Eats promo codes, new user offers, and Uber One discounts to slash your delivery fees and meal costs.
entries.content:
Uber began as a modern alternative to taxis, letting riders order through a phone app, track the driver’s route in real time, share their location with contacts, and even split the fare in the app—it was the convenience-obsessed answer to the old way of hailing cabs. Then in 2014, Uber leveled up with Uber Eats. Much like Uber was the convenient, modern answer to taxis, Uber Eats was the equivalent for food delivery.

Instead of calling a local restaurant and enlisting a delivery driver from that restaurant, Uber Eats draws from hundreds of participating restaurants, cafes, and stores in your area, tailoring deals and picks to your location and preferences. So if you want fresh sushi from your favorite local spot for a date night in, or just need some Advil and Gatorade after a night out, Uber Eats delivers the goods in minutes flat. Whether you’re new to the service or a longtime devotee, we have an Uber Eats promo code and other Uber Eats coupon codes to help you save big—and stay at home.

Uber Eats Coupon Code for New Users

One of the easiest ways to save big on Uber Eats is to create a new account. First-time Uber customers can save 30 to 50% on their first order, plus new offers with up to $20 off rides or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber Eats promo code to get this steep discount—this offer applies automatically when you create your account and book your first trip or delivery.

Save More With Uber One Membership

If you use the rideshare app often or order takeout multiple nights a week, an Uber One membership will pay for itself within a few weeks. At $10 per month, it offers major perks that add up over time if you use the service frequently. You’ll get tons of perks across rides and food delivery, including $0 delivery fees on eligible food, grocery, and retail orders, up to 10% off eligible Uber Eats orders, 5% back in Uber One credits on eligible rides, and automatic surge savings. Uber One members save $29 on average every month.

Uber Eats Promo Code: 50% Off Your First Uber Ride

As mentioned above, the simplest way to save big with Uber is to be a first-time user. You’ll save 30 to 50% on your first ride, including up to $20 off all rides or $15 off Uber Eats orders. You don’t even need an Uber promo code. Uber welcome discounts apply automatically once you create your account and book your first trip. Trust me, you’ll get used to the convenience of a rideshare app and a food and delivery service app, all in one place—in the palm of your hand.

Share the Gift of an Uber Eats Gift Card

One of my go-to gifts lately is an Uber Eats gift card. I find it especially thoughtful and useful as a convenience gift, whether that’s after a death, loss, birth, or a big life change. An Uber Eats gift card is more than just a gift card. It takes another thing off someone’s plate and offers an easy, comforting meal, especially during times of grief or celebration. Uber Eats gift cards start at $15 and can be purchased from participating retailers or sent instantly through the app to friends and family.

Unlock an Uber Eats Student Discount

Being a student often means tight budgets, long nights, and limited kitchen space (and culinary knowledge). Investing in an Uber One account may be a good idea—for only $10 per month, you can get, on average, $30 in savings on Uber rides and Uber grocery and meal delivery. You won’t have to worry about meal planning or expensive takeout bills. With Uber One discounts and promos, you can get multiple meals for the week at a lower cost. And if you’re a student, you can try Uber One for free for four weeks to make sure the service is a fit. After that, the service is half off at only $5 per month. No Uber Eats coupon code necessary. Just verify your student status to get the four weeks for free and $5 per month after.

Get Your Groceries Delivered with Uber Eats

If you’re not in the mood to eat out, stay in and get groceries delivered with Uber Eats. Uber Eats partners with hundreds of grocery stores near you—including your favorite supermarkets—for same-day delivery in as little as 25 minutes. Using your location, Uber Eats offers fast delivery from drugstores, grocery chains, and local stores, so whether you need toilet paper or a gallon of milk, Uber Eats delivers.

Deliver With Uber Eats

If you’re looking for a side hustle or gig work where you set your own schedule, delivering with Uber Eats is a great way to earn extra cash. It's flexible in so many ways. You can deliver with a car, a bike, or on foot, for an hour, a day, or daily. Uber Eats makes it easy to see what you’ll earn and what your day will look like. You’ll be able to see how much you’ll earn by delivering before you accept a job, and the tips you get are all yours. With Instant Pay, you can cash out up to 6 times a day for a fee, and weekly earnings are automatically transferred to your bank account. The possibilities (and flexibility) are endless—you can sign up to deliver food and packages, as well as “Shop & Deliver,” which allows you to earn by shopping for customers and delivering the order.

Get Your Starbucks Delivered With Uber Eats

If you’re like me and need about 40 oz of coffee to get through the day, you know how important it is to have caffeine at a moment’s notice. With Uber Eats’ vast network, you can now get your Starbucks delivered. Starbucks delivery with Uber Eats couldn’t be easier. There are hundreds of Starbucks locations across the country, with both delivery and pickup available through the convenient app. Enter your zip code to see the nearest matching pickup location. Whether you’re catering for a big meeting or just want a quick breakfast.

FAQs

In the app, go to your account menu, select "Promotions" (or "Add promo/gift card" at checkout), enter the code, and it should apply automatically if valid and still active.

Find Your Perfect Peacock Plan

Like other streaming services, Peacock offers plans for every type of binge-watcher. Their subscription tiers let you customize based on what you’ll actually watch and your budget: Select, for $8 per month; Premium, for $11 per month, which includes Peacock’s catalog, live sports, current NBC and Bravo shows, and over 50 channels. Premium Plus is $17 per month or $170 per year and includes: no ads, the ability to download titles to watch offline, and access to your local NBC channel live 24/7. Peacock Premium includes over 80k hours of streaming, with new and old shows, films, and originals, live sports, currently running NBC and Bravo shows (OG Real Housewives fans know), and over 50 channels that are always streaming something. The Premium Plus plan includes everything I just mentioned, plus no ads (a huge W for people who chronically get on their phones during commercials and forget to pay attention when the show comes back on). Check out the full details on the differing Peacock plans to figure out which is right for you.
